message.content:
Below is a concise overview of the key rights and protections you have as a tenant in Texas. (This is general information and not legal advice; for specific situations you may want to consult an attorney or a local tenant‑rights organization.) | Area | What the law says | Practical Tips | |------|-------------------|----------------| | **Security Deposit** | • Landlords may charge a security deposit, but it must be returned within 30 days after you move out, unless you give written notice of intent to stay.
• The deposit can only be used for unpaid rent, damages beyond normal wear, or cleaning if the lease specifies it. | • Keep a copy of the lease and any move‑in inspection checklist.
• Take photos or videos of the unit before you move in and after you move out. | | **Habitability** | • Texas law requires landlords to keep the premises in a habitable condition (e.g., plumbing, heating, structural safety).
• Landlords must repair major problems within a reasonable time after you notify them. | • Report problems in writing (email or text) and keep a copy.
• If repairs are not made, you may withhold rent or pay the repair yourself and deduct the cost from your rent (but do this only after following the proper procedure). | | **Rent Payment** | • Rent is due on the date specified in the lease.
• Late fees are allowed only if the lease states them and they are reasonable. | • Pay on time or negotiate a payment plan if you’re having trouble. | | **Right to Quiet Enjoyment** | • Landlords cannot enter the unit without proper notice (usually 24–48 hrs) except in emergencies. | • Keep a log of any unannounced entries. | | **Privacy** | • Landlords must respect your privacy; they can’t monitor your activities or tamper with your personal belongings. | • If you suspect surveillance, document it and consider contacting local authorities. | | **Discrimination** | • Under federal Fair Housing laws and Texas statutes, landlords cannot discriminate based on race, color, religion, sex, national origin, familial status, disability, or source of income. | • If you believe you’ve been discriminated against, file a complaint with the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD) or the Texas Commission on Human Rights. | | **Lease Termination** | • Either party can terminate a lease with proper notice (usually 30 days for month‑to‑month leases).
• Landlords must provide a written notice of termination. | • Keep copies of all notices. | | **Eviction Process** | • Landlords must follow the Texas eviction procedure: serve a written notice (e.g., 3‑day notice for non‑payment), file a lawsuit, and obtain a court order.
• You have the right to contest the eviction in court. | • Respond promptly to notices.
• Seek legal aid if you’re facing eviction. | | **Repair and Deduct** | • If the landlord fails to repair a major problem, you may pay the repair yourself and deduct the cost from your rent, but you must follow the lease’s repair‑and‑deduct clause and provide receipts. | • Keep receipts and document the issue. | | **Subletting** | • The lease may allow or prohibit subletting. If allowed, you must follow the lease terms. | • Get written permission if required. | | **Utilities** | • The lease should specify who pays utilities. | • Verify utility responsibilities before signing. | | **Insurance** | • Landlords are not required to provide renter’s insurance, but it’s highly recommended. | • Consider a basic policy covering personal property and liability. | | **Legal Resources** | • Texas Attorney General’s Office – Consumer Protection Division.
• Texas Department of Housing and Community Affairs.
• Local tenant‑rights groups (e.g., Texas Tenants Union). | • Use these resources for disputes or to learn more about your rights. | ### Quick Checklist Before Signing a Lease 1. **Read the lease thoroughly** – look for clauses on security deposits, repairs, late fees, and notice periods. 2. **Ask about habitability** – confirm that the landlord will maintain plumbing, heating, and structural integrity. 3. **Confirm utility responsibilities** – who pays water, gas, electric, internet? 4. **Check for discrimination clauses** – ensure the lease complies with fair housing laws. 5. **Get everything in writing** – verbal agreements are harder to enforce. --- #### When Things Go Wrong | Issue | First Step | Next Step | |-------|------------|-----------| | Landlord refuses to make repairs | Write a formal notice (email or letter) and keep a copy | If no response in 10–14 days, consider filing a complaint with the Texas Department of Housing and Community Affairs or a local housing agency | | Unreasonable late fee | Review the lease; if the fee is excessive, discuss it with the landlord | If unresolved, seek mediation or legal advice | | Unlawful eviction notice | Verify the notice meets Texas requirements (e.g., 3‑day notice for non‑payment) | File a defense in the county court where the eviction was served | | Discrimination claim | Gather evidence (emails, witnesses) | File a complaint with HUD or the Texas Commission on Human Rights | --- **Bottom line:** As a Texas tenant, you have the right to a safe, habitable home, privacy, and protection from discrimination. Keep records, communicate in writing, and know the legal steps you can take if your landlord violates your rights. If you’re ever unsure, reach out to a local tenant‑rights organization or an attorney who specializes in landlord‑tenant law.
